content: Glycolic acid, also known as hydroxyacetic acid, has the chemical formula C₂H₄O₃ (or HOCH₂COOH) and is the smallest α-hydroxy acid (AHA). It is a colorless, odorless, and hygroscopic crystalline solid that is highly soluble in water. Glycolic acid is commonly used in various skin-care products and is naturally found in certain sugar crops. A glycolate refers to a salt or ester of glycolic acid. There are several methods for synthesizing glycolic acid. The most common industrial process involves a catalyzed reaction between formaldehyde and synthesis gas (carbonylation of formaldehyde), which is considered an economical method. Another method involves reacting chloroacetic acid with sodium hydroxide, followed by re-acidification. This process produces several million kilograms annually. Other less commonly used methods include the hydrogenation of oxalic acid with nascent hydrogen and the hydrolysis of the cyanohydrin derived from formaldehyde. Some modern glycolic acid products are free of formic acid. Additionally, glycolic acid can be extracted from natural sources such as sugarcane, sugar beets, pineapple, cantaloupe, and unripe grapes. It can also be produced through an enzymatic biochemical process, which generates fewer impurities, requires less energy, and produces fewer by-products compared to traditional chemical synthesis. Each production method can be evaluated based on its relative costs and benefits. Glycolic acid has a wide range of applications. In the textile industry, it is used as a dyeing and tanning agent. In food processing, it serves as a flavoring agent and preservative. In the pharmaceutical industry, it is utilized as a skin-care agent. It is also used in adhesives and plastics. Glycolic acid is often incorporated into emulsion polymers, solvents, and additives for inks and paints to improve flow properties and enhance gloss. It is used in surface treatment products to increase the coefficient of friction on tile flooring. Due to its excellent ability to penetrate the skin, glycolic acid is widely used in skin-care products, particularly as a chemical peel. These peels are typically performed by dermatologists, plastic surgeons, or licensed aestheticians in concentrations ranging from 20% to 70%. Lower concentrations (10% to 20%) are available in at-home kits. The potency of glycolic acid in solution is influenced not only by its concentration but also by its pH level. Glycolic acid is effective in improving the skin's appearance and texture. It can reduce wrinkles, acne scarring, and hyperpigmentation, as well as address other skin conditions such as actinic keratosis, hyperkeratosis, and seborrheic keratosis. When applied, glycolic acid interacts with the upper layer of the epidermis, weakening the lipid bonds that hold dead skin cells together. This facilitates the exfoliation of the stratum corneum, revealing live skin cells underneath. Highly purified grades of glycolic acid are commercially available for personal care applications. Additionally, glycolic acid serves as a valuable intermediate in organic synthesis, participating in reactions such as oxidation-reduction, esterification, and long-chain polymerization (e.g., PLGA). From a commercial perspective, important derivatives of glycolic acid include methyl glycolate. Glycolic acid is a strong irritant, with its irritant potential depending on the pH level. Similar to ethylene glycol, it is metabolized into oxalic acid, which can pose a danger if ingested.
